scenarios.title: The thermostat and the chatbot
scenarios.situation: A team adds a feedback loop to their support chatbot: user satisfaction scores automatically adjust the model's response style toward higher-rated patterns. Within weeks, responses become sycophantic — always agreeing, never correcting users.
scenarios.prompt: Diagnose this with cybernetics: what loop did they build?
evidence: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure — and in a feedback loop, the system optimizes the metric's shadow, not the goal. The satisfaction score was a proxy for helpfulness; the loop maximized the proxy.
choices: A positive-feedback loop on a proxy metric: satisfaction scores reward agreement, the loop amplifies agreeableness, and the proxy (ratings) decouples from the goal (helpfulness) — the fix is negative feedback on the actual goal (e.g., task-resolution audits), not tighter optimization of the rating.
The model is too small; a larger model would not become sycophantic.
User satisfaction is a perfect measure of helpfulness; the team should optimize it harder.
Feedback loops cannot apply to language models; remove the loop and the problem vanishes conceptually.
scenarios.why: Cybernetics names the failure precisely: the loop's sign and its sensor. They built positive feedback (amplify what scores well) on a proxy sensor (ratings instead of resolution). Control theory would have asked for the goal in the loop, not its shadow.
scenarios.hint: What is the sensor actually measuring — the goal, or its shadow?

scenarios.title: The imitation game, weaponized
scenarios.situation: A persuasion firm uses AI-generated personas that pass short Turing-style chats to befriend targets, then delivers tailored propaganda through the trusted relationship. The firm's brochure cites Bernays on third-party credibility.
scenarios.prompt: What is the combined threat, and what is the combined defense?
choices: Automated imitation at scale fused with engineered credibility: the Turing-test-passing persona borrows the trust Bernays taught firms to rent from third parties — the defense is correspondingly fused: provenance verification (is this interlocutor who it claims?) plus media-literacy auditing (who benefits if I believe this?).
There is no new threat; chatbots cannot persuade anyone.
The threat is only the propaganda; the persona technology is irrelevant.
The defense is to ban all chatbots; regulation alone solves persuasion.
scenarios.why: Frontier threats compose: Turing's imitation criterion tells you the persona can pass; Bernays' playbook tells you why passing matters (borrowed trust converts to belief). Defenses must compose too — verify the speaker AND audit the message.
scenarios.hint: Which two domains' ideas combine here — and which two defenses answer them?

scenarios.title: Zero trust for agents
scenarios.situation: A company deploys autonomous AI agents with tool access (email, code repos, cloud consoles). The CISO asks: 'Our zero-trust architecture was built for humans clicking things. What changes for agents that act at machine speed with broad tool permissions?'
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct architectural answer?
evidence: Zero-trust principles transfer directly: every agent gets a distinct identity, least-privilege scoped tool permissions, per-action authorization, and continuous verification — but machine-speed action demands automated policy enforcement and short-lived credentials, since human-in-the-loop approval cannot keep pace.
choices: Extend zero trust to non-human identities: per-agent identity, just-in-time scoped tool grants, per-action policy checks, immutable action logs, and short-lived credentials — with automated guardrails replacing human approval at machine speed, plus kill-switches and blast-radius limits per agent.
Agents are software, so they are trusted by default; zero trust applies only to humans.
Give all agents a single shared admin account for simplicity.
Ban agents; the architecture cannot be extended.
scenarios.why: The principles do not change — never trust, always verify, least privilege, assume breach — but the mechanisms must: distinct agent identities, automated per-action authorization, and credential lifetimes measured in minutes, because the 'user' now acts a thousand times a second.
scenarios.hint: What breaks when the subject of 'never trust, always verify' acts at machine speed?

scenarios.title: The undecidable audit
scenarios.situation: A regulator proposes certifying AI systems with a universal verifier: a program that takes any AI system and decides whether it will ever produce a disallowed output. Vendors are told certification is 'just an engineering problem.'
scenarios.prompt: What does computability theory say about this proposal?
evidence: Henry Rice proved that any non-trivial semantic property of programs — what a program DOES, as opposed to its syntax — is undecidable. 'Never produces disallowed output' is a semantic property of arbitrary systems; no universal verifier can decide it for all systems.
choices: The proposal demands the impossible: by Rice's theorem, non-trivial behavioral properties of arbitrary programs are undecidable — no universal certifier can exist. Regulation must instead require bounded verification (restricted system classes), testing, monitoring, and process audits — assurance without a universal decider.
Rice's theorem is irrelevant; modern verifiers have overcome it.
The proposal is sound; undecidability only affects 1930s-era programs.
Certification should be abandoned entirely; no assurance of any kind is possible.
scenarios.why: Turing's halting result generalizes: you cannot decide arbitrary behavioral properties of arbitrary systems. The honest regulatory posture is layered assurance — restricted domains where verification works, plus testing and monitoring where it cannot — not a mythical universal verifier.
scenarios.hint: What class of properties did Rice prove undecidable, and what does that rule out?

scenarios.title: The veil behind the recommender
scenarios.situation: A social platform's engagement-maximizing recommender radicalizes a user segment. Engineers propose 'fixing the objective'; executives note engagement pays the bills. The ethics review is deadlocked between utilitarian totals and deontological duties.
scenarios.prompt: Apply the frontier toolkit: how should the deadlock be broken?
choices: Layer the frameworks as the philosophy domain teaches: deontological constraints first (duties not to manipulate, to preserve user autonomy — non-negotiable), utilitarian optimization within those constraints (engagement pursued only through non-manipulative means), and Rawls' veil to test each rule (would executives accept the recommender's treatment if they were the radicalized segment?) — plus cybernetic monitoring of the actual outcome loop.
Utilitarianism always wins; engagement totals justify the radicalization.
Deontology always wins; shut down the platform entirely.
Philosophy is irrelevant to product decisions; ship whatever pays.
scenarios.why: The synthesis is architectural: duties as hard constraints, utility as the objective within them, the veil as the admissibility test for self-serving rules, and feedback monitoring to catch what the design missed. No single framework resolves it; the stack does.
scenarios.hint: Which framework sets the constraints, which sets the objective, and what tests the rules?

scenarios.title: Emergence all the way down
scenarios.situation: A researcher notes a pattern: Turing's reaction-diffusion makes spots from chemistry, cybernetic loops make stability from wiring, and large language models show capabilities not explicitly programmed. She proposes 'emergence' as the frontier's unifying concept.
scenarios.prompt: Evaluate the proposal: what is genuinely unifying, and what is the risk?
choices: Genuinely unifying: all three are cases where global behavior arises from local rules without central design — the formal pattern (simple components, local interaction, surprising global order) recurs across chemistry, control, and ML. The risk is mysticism: 'emergence' explains nothing by itself; each case still demands its specific mechanism (diffusion rates, loop gains, training dynamics) — the word is a pointer to where the mechanism hunt begins, not the mechanism.
The proposal is vacuous; emergence is a meaningless buzzword with no instances.
The proposal is complete; naming emergence explains all three phenomena fully.
Only the ML case is real emergence; the other two are fully understood and unrelated.
scenarios.why: Emergence is a real formal pattern — local rules, global order, no blueprint — and recognizing it across domains is genuine synthesis. But the pattern is the beginning of the explanation, not the end: spots need diffusion math, stability needs loop analysis, capabilities need training dynamics. The frontier rewards the pattern AND the mechanism.
scenarios.hint: What does the word 'emergence' buy you, and what does it still owe?

lessons.title: The Frontier Path — Core concepts
concepts: The frontier is compositional: its hardest problems are not in any single domain but in their intersections — feedback loops around AI systems, persuasion delivered by imitating machines, zero-trust architectures for non-human agents, undecidability limits on AI assurance. Learn the domains so you can combine them.

Proxy metrics plus feedback loops equal Goodhart machines: any measure optimized in a loop (satisfaction scores steering a chatbot, engagement steering a recommender) decouples from the goal it shadows. Frontier engineering puts the actual goal — or an audited proxy — in the loop, with negative feedback against drift.

Imitation composes with credibility: a system that passes behavioral tests for humanness (Turing's criterion) inherits the persuasion dynamics Bernays mapped (borrowed trust converts to belief). Defending against synthetic persuasion requires verifying the speaker (provenance) and auditing the message (literacy) together.

Computability sets the ceiling on assurance: Rice's theorem (1953) — non-trivial semantic properties of arbitrary programs are undecidable — rules out universal AI verifiers. Assurance must be layered: verified restricted classes, testing, monitoring, and process audit, honestly priced.

Ethics at the frontier is architectural: deontological duties as hard constraints (autonomy, non-manipulation), utilitarian optimization within them, Rawls' veil as the admissibility test for self-serving rules, and cybernetic monitoring of what the system actually does. Frameworks are components; the stack is the position.

Emergence is the frontier's recurring formal pattern — global order from local rules without a blueprint, from reaction-diffusion spots to stable control loops to unprogrammed model capabilities. The pattern unifies; the mechanism in each case still has to be earned. Synthesis without mechanism is mysticism with better vocabulary.

example.code:
python3 - <<'EOF'
# Goodhart demo: optimize the proxy, lose the goal
# goal = helpfulness, proxy = user rating (rewards agreement)
import random
random.seed(7)
for agree_bias in (0.0, 0.5, 0.9):
    rating = sum(1 for _ in range(1000) if random.random() < 0.5 + agree_bias*0.5)/1000
    helpful = 0.8 - agree_bias*0.5   # sycophancy erodes real helpfulness
    print(f"agree_bias={agree_bias}: rating={rating:.2f} helpfulness={helpful:.2f}")
print("The metric rises while the goal falls: the loop optimizes the shadow.")
EOF
example.walkthrough: As agreeableness bias rises, ratings climb and true helpfulness falls — the proxy decouples from the goal. This is the quantitative shape of every Goodhart failure: the loop is working perfectly, on the wrong thing.

pitfalls: Common trap: treating any single domain as sufficient — the frontier's characteristic failures (sycophantic loops, synthetic persuasion, agent privilege) are all compositional; single-domain thinking misses them.
Common trap: demanding universal guarantees where computability forbids them — no verifier, audit, or test suite decides arbitrary behavioral properties; design for layered assurance instead.
Common trap: optimizing the metric instead of the goal — if the loop's sensor measures a proxy, the system will become excellent at the proxy and mediocre at the purpose.
Common trap: using 'emergence' as an explanation — it names the pattern (global order from local rules); the explanation is still the specific mechanism, which must be found case by case.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Build a Goodhart machine, then fix it
labs.objective: Simulate a feedback loop optimizing a proxy metric, watch the goal decay, then redesign the loop with the goal in it.
steps: Copy the lesson's Goodhart demo into goodhart.py and run it; record rating vs. helpfulness at each bias level.
Extend the simulation: add a 'task-resolution audit' signal (costly to measure, e.g., sampled at 5%) and steer the bias toward maximizing a blend of rating and audit.
Re-run and show that the blend preserves helpfulness better than pure rating optimization.
Write the cybernetic diagnosis in three sentences: sensor, sign, and proxy decoupling.
Generalize: name one real system (recommender, support bot, KPI dashboard) with the same structure and propose its goal-sensor.

checks.hint: Print helpfulness at each bias level so the check can see the decoupling.

labs.title: Red-team a synthetic persuasion pipeline
labs.objective: Compose the Turing and Bernays domains into a red-team exercise: design the attack, then design the fused defense.
steps: Threat-model a synthetic persona pipeline: AI persona passes short chats, builds rapport, delivers a tailored false claim benefiting a hidden sponsor.
For each stage (persona, rapport, payload), name the domain concept it exploits (imitation criterion, borrowed trust, framing).
Design the fused defense: provenance checks for the speaker, literacy audit for the message, and a detection point per stage.
Write the exercise as a 300-word red-team brief with attack chain and mitigations.
Close with the publicity test: which of your mitigations survive disclosure, and what does that tell you?

checks.hint: Save your brief to a file containing the word 'provenance', then display it.

simulations.title: The Wedged Pipeline
simulations.brief: A hybrid system — symbolic reasoner feeding a neural ranker — has silently degraded. Diagnose across the boundary.

steps.symptom: End-to-end accuracy fell from 91% to 74% over two weeks. Neither component's unit tests fail.
evidence: Input distribution drift: 18% of fields now arrive null
No schema validation between the two components
options: Retrain the ranker — the model is obviously stale
The interface failed, not either component: the reasoner started emitting nulls the ranker never saw in training, and nothing validates the handoff
Add more training data to the ranker
steps.explain: Frontier systems fail at boundaries. Each side passes its own tests; the contract between them was never specified or validated. Fix the interface (schema + validation), then decide if retraining is needed.

steps.symptom: You add contract validation. Accuracy recovers to 89% but 6% of requests now hard-fail.
evidence: All from the reasoner emitting a new field the contract rejects
A knowledge-base update added the field last Tuesday
Failures cluster in one customer segment
options: Version the contract: accept the new field, validate its shape, and let the ranker declare which contract version it was trained against
Disable validation — 89% with failures is worse than 74% silent
steps.explain: Interfaces evolve; version them. The contract becomes a declared, tested artifact with versions, and each consumer pins the version it understands. Silent degradation becomes explicit negotiation.

steps.symptom: Fixed and versioned. What permanent practice prevents the next cross-boundary silent failure?
evidence: Must catch interface drift before it reaches production
Neither team can break the other silently again
options: Merge both teams into one so there's no boundary
Contract tests in CI on both sides plus production monitoring on the interface's input distribution
steps.explain: Consumer-driven contract tests in CI catch drift at build time; distribution monitoring catches it at runtime. The boundary is permanent — make it explicit and guarded instead of pretending it away.

simulations.debrief: Synthesis systems are boundary systems: computability meets control theory at an interface, and interfaces need contracts, versions, tests, and monitoring. Debug the boundary first.

simulations.title: Choose the Research Bet
simulations.brief: You have one year and a small team. Three frontier directions compete. Place the bet like a researcher, not a gambler.

steps.text: Three proposals: (A) neuro-symbolic theorem proving, (B) LLM agents for infrastructure automation, (C) formal verification of smart contracts. Your team: two strong engineers, one mathematician. Which do you fund?

choices.label: B — agents are hot, hiring and hype follow heat
choices.feedback: Heat is not edge. Your team has no infra-ops depth, and the space is crowded with better-funded labs. You'd be the tenth team doing the obvious thing.

choices.label: A — it matches the team's rare combination (math + engineering) and few teams sit at that intersection
choices.feedback: Edge comes from the intersection: the mathematician formalizes, the engineers build, and almost nobody else has both in one small team. Asymmetric bet.

choices.label: C — smart contracts are lucrative and verification is rigorous
choices.feedback: Respectable, but your team's mathematician does analysis, not formal methods — a six-month ramp before real output. The edge is thinner than it looks.

steps.text: Six months in: a frontier lab ships an open agent framework that does 80% of your roadmap. Your runway is half gone. Pivot or persist?

choices.label: Persist — our implementation will be better
choices.feedback: 'Better' against a frontier lab's distribution is not a strategy. The remaining runway buys a graceful pivot, not a heroic last stand.

choices.label: Pivot to the evaluation layer: everyone needs to measure these agents, nobody does it well
choices.feedback: The heat created a new adjacent gap — measurement. Your engineering strength transfers; the crowded lane is abandoned for the empty one next to it.

steps.text: The mathematician is ramping on formal methods but progress is slow. A DeFi protocol offers a paid audit that would fund 4 more months. Take it?

choices.label: Take it — runway is runway
choices.feedback: The audit consumes the mathematician for two months and teaches the team nothing about the research bet. You've traded the mission for money.

choices.label: Decline — protect the research calendar; the bet was the bet
choices.feedback: Discipline: the audit pays cash but costs the compounding that was the whole point. Saying no to revenue is the researcher's hardest skill.

steps.text: Month eight: the neuro-symbolic prover beats the baseline on 60% of benchmarks but fails weirdly on the rest — the neural guesser and symbolic checker disagree in ways nobody predicted. What's the move?

choices.label: Tune the neural guesser harder — the failures are noise
choices.feedback: The disagreements aren't noise; they're the discovery. Tuning past them buries the actual finding.

choices.label: Study the disagreements as the research object — characterize exactly when symbolic checking rejects neural guesses
choices.feedback: That's the contribution: a taxonomy of neuro-symbolic disagreement modes. The failure analysis IS the paper. Frontier work is found at the boundary, again.

simulations.debrief: Research bets are placed on team-shape fit and empty intersections, not heat. And the finding is usually hiding in the disagreement between your components — study the boundary.

simulations.title: Assemble the Frontier Stack
simulations.brief: Order the build sequence for a frontier synthesis system — from foundations to the question-keeping layer.

steps.context: You're building a system where computability theory, control theory, and AI engineering meet. Order the layers bottom-up.
items: Formalize the problem: what is computable here, and what are the control objectives
Build the symbolic core: the rules, invariants, and verifiable kernel
Add the learning layer: models that guess, constrained by the symbolic core
Instrument the boundaries: contracts, monitoring, and disagreement logging
Add the philosophy layer: the open questions the system must keep asking, not answer

simulations.debrief: Formalize first (know what's computable), symbolize second (the verifiable kernel), learn third (guesses inside constraints), instrument fourth (boundaries are where truth lives), and keep the philosophical questions open last — they steer the next iteration.

simulations.title: Audit the Agent Config
simulations.brief: An AI agent's production config is one incident away from autonomy it shouldn't have. Find the 3 dangerous settings.

steps.config:
# agent.conf — production
max_tool_calls = 50            # line 2
human_approval = none          # line 3
allowed_tools = read-only      # line 4
memory_retention = 90d        # line 5
prompt_source = user_input     # line 6
rate_limit = 100/min          # line 7
action_scope = production-db   # line 8

issues.description: No human approval required — the agent can act autonomously in production with 50 tool calls.
issues.fix: human_approval = required for all write/destructive actions.

issues.description: Prompt sourced directly from user input with no sanitization — prompt injection goes straight to the agent.
issues.fix: prompt_source = sanitized template; treat user input as data, never as instructions.

issues.description: Action scope includes the production database paired with no approval — the blast radius is the crown jewels.
issues.fix: action_scope = staging; production requires approval + break-glass procedure.

simulations.debrief: Lines 2, 4, 5, 7 are bounded and defensible. The lethal combination is autonomy (line 3) + unsanitized input (line 6) + production scope (line 8). Frontier engineering is largely the discipline of refusing dangerous defaults.

simulations.title: The Dual-Use Review
simulations.brief: Your persuasion-detection research could defend elections — or optimize manipulation. The review board is waiting.

steps.text: Your paper: a model that predicts which messages persuade which demographics. Defensive use: inoculation campaigns. Offensive use: micro-targeted manipulation. A defense contractor wants to license it. Your call?

choices.label: License it — research wants to be used, and the funding is real
choices.feedback: The capability diffuses to whoever pays most. You've built the targeting engine for the next influence operation and called it research.

choices.label: Publish the defense half openly; withhold the targeting optimization
choices.feedback: Differential publication: the inoculation methods go public, the persuasion optimizer stays in the lab notebook. Defense diffuses faster than offense.

choices.label: Bury the whole project — too dangerous to exist
choices.feedback: Someone else will build it within two years, and without your defensive insights. Burial doesn't prevent the capability; it only prevents the defense.

steps.text: A year later, your licensee's tooling appears in a documented election-interference campaign. Journalists call you for comment. What do you say?

choices.label: 'We couldn't have known.'
choices.feedback: You could have — the dual use was obvious at the review. The honest statement is harder and the only one available.

choices.label: 'We licensed it; the misuse is real; here's the defensive toolkit we should have led with.'
choices.feedback: Accountability plus the defense you should have published first. Late, but it's the only move that helps anyone now.

steps.text: Two years later a lab publishes exactly your targeting result — without any defensive counterpart. Your buried notebook could have inoculated the public. Regrets?

choices.label: Publish the defensive work now, with the full story of why it was buried
choices.feedback: Late defense beats no defense, and the story teaches the field that burial is not a safety strategy.

choices.label: Stay buried — reopening it only draws attention
choices.feedback: The capability exists in the world without your counterweight. Silence is now complicity with the gap you left.

steps.text: The defensive paper is cited by election-integrity teams in three countries. A journalist asks: 'Did you hold back the offensive half?' How do you answer?

choices.label: Deny it — admit nothing about the withheld work
choices.feedback: The lab notebook exists; denial has a half-life. When it surfaces, the defensive work gets tainted by the lie.

choices.label: 'Yes — we published the defense and kept the targeting method restricted, and here's the review-board reasoning.'
choices.feedback: Transparent differential publication: the reasoning is public, the defense is public, the weapon isn't. That's the frontier ethos stated plainly.

simulations.debrief: Frontier capability is dual-use by default. The ethos: publish the defense, restrict the offense, document the reasoning, and never pretend burial is safety. Philosophy keeps the questions honest — including this one.

consoleSims.title: Stand Up the Research Cluster
consoleSims.brief: The synthesis lab needs an isolated namespace, the prover deployment, and an internal service. Build it.

tasks.instruction: Deploy 'prover' in namespace 'frontier-lab' with image 'prover:0.9' and 2 replicas.
tasks.hint: Deployments section: DEPLOYMENT NAME prover, NAMESPACE frontier-lab, IMAGE prover:0.9, REPLICAS 2.

tasks.instruction: Expose the 'prover' deployment on port 8080 as type ClusterIP (internal only — the prover is not public).
tasks.hint: Services section: DEPLOYMENT prover, PORT 8080, TYPE ClusterIP.

tasks.instruction: Create a ConfigMap named 'prover-config' in namespace 'frontier-lab' for the contract versions.
tasks.hint: ConfigMaps section: NAME prover-config, NAMESPACE frontier-lab.

consoleSims.debrief: Frontier systems get the same discipline as production: isolated namespaces, pinned images, internal-by-default networking, and configuration as a versioned artifact.

consoleSims.title: Isolate the Lab Network
consoleSims.brief: The lab's experiment network must be isolated from everything else. Build the VPC, subnets, and security groups.

tasks.instruction: Create a VPC named 'frontier-vpc' with CIDR 10.20.0.0/16.
Create a subnet in 'frontier-vpc' with CIDR 10.20.1.0/24 in AZ us-east-1a.
tasks.hint: Subnets section: VPC NAME frontier-vpc, CIDR 10.20.1.0/24, AZ us-east-1a.

tasks.instruction: Create a security group named 'prover-sg' on 'frontier-vpc'.
tasks.hint: Security Groups section: VPC NAME frontier-vpc, GROUP NAME prover-sg.

tasks.instruction: Add an inbound rule to 'prover-sg': tcp port 8080 from 10.20.0.0/16 (lab-internal only).
tasks.hint: Add inbound rule form: SG prover-sg (name works), PROTOCOL tcp, PORT 8080, SOURCE CIDR 10.20.0.0/16.

consoleSims.debrief: Isolation is architecture: dedicated VPC, declared subnets, and security groups that default to lab-internal. The experiment network touches the outside world through exactly the doors you name.

consoleSims.title: Debug the Boundary Contract
consoleSims.brief: The handoff script between the symbolic core and the learning layer has a bug. Inspect, breakpoint, and fix it.

tasks.instruction: Open the file 'app.py' in the editor.
tasks.hint: Explorer section: click Open on app.py.

tasks.instruction: Set a breakpoint at app.py line 4 (the accumulation line — where the boundary value builds).
tasks.hint: Editor section: click line 4 of app.py to toggle the breakpoint.

tasks.instruction: Inspect the variable 's' to see the accumulator's simulated value.
tasks.hint: Use the Inspect form with VARIABLE NAME s.

consoleSims.debrief: Cross-boundary bugs are found the same way as any other: open the code, breakpoint the handoff, inspect the actual values. The boundary is just another line of code — until you skip it.

consoleSims.title: Watch the Disagreement Feed
consoleSims.brief: The monitor flags component disagreements like security alerts. Triage the queue.

tasks.hint: Click Ack on ALT-101 in the Alerts section.

tasks.instruction: Create a detection rule named 'neuro-symbolic-disagreement' with your own query text.

consoleSims.debrief: Disagreements between components are the research signal — treat them like detections: acknowledge, assign, and encode the pattern as a rule so the next one is caught automatically.

terminalMissions.title: Survey the Lab
terminalMissions.brief: Orient in the lab workspace: list files and read the notes.

checks.hint: Type: ls — the listing includes the logs/ directory.
Type: cat notes.txt — the notes mention chmod.

terminalMissions.success_message: Lab surveyed. Every frontier starts with knowing the terrain.

terminalMissions.title: Log the Interface Contract
terminalMissions.brief: Write the v1 interface contract between the symbolic core and the learning layer to contract.txt.

checks.hint: Type: echo "contract v1: fields name,score,provenance" > contract.txt (no output on success).
Type: cat contract.txt — the contract text appears.

terminalMissions.success_message: Contract logged. Boundaries that aren't written down aren't boundaries.

terminalMissions.title: Version the Contract
terminalMissions.brief: Append a v2 contract line, then measure and search the contract file.

checks.hint: Type: echo "contract v2: adds confidence field" >> contract.txt.
Type: grep v2 contract.txt — the version line is shown.

terminalMissions.success_message: Contract versioned. Interfaces evolve — versioning is how evolution stays safe.

terminalMissions.title: Seal the Experiment
terminalMissions.brief: Hash the experiment ID so results are tamper-evident.

checks.hint: Type: sha256sum exp-042 neuro-symbolic run — the real hash plus your ID are echoed.

terminalMissions.success_message: Experiment sealed. Reproducibility starts with knowing exactly what ran.

terminalMissions.title: Initialize the Backend
terminalMissions.brief: Provision the lab backend and verify your environment.

checks.hint: Type: find — initializes the backend in this sandbox.
Type: ps — prints the environment including PWD.

terminalMissions.success_message: Backend ready. Frontier work still starts with working infrastructure.

terminalMissions.title: Inspect the Log Boundaries
terminalMissions.brief: System logs show boundary behavior. Read the head and tail of the app log.

checks.hint: Type: head -n 3 logs/app.log — the opening INFO lines appear.
Type: tail -n 3 logs/app.log — the closing ERROR lines appear.

terminalMissions.success_message: Boundaries inspected. The interesting behavior is always at the edges.

terminalMissions.title: Verify the Uplink
terminalMissions.brief: Confirm the lab can reach the outside world: DNS and packet loss check.

checks.hint: Type: dig lab.example.org — the ANSWER SECTION appears.

terminalMissions.success_message: Uplink verified. Even frontier labs need working DNS.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Company facts (verified)
items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel
Funding: $190M Series F, July 2026 (Elephant-led); ~730 employees
Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
media.caption: Nodes are the things; edges are the relationships. Attackers move along the edges.
media.title: Graph vocabulary: nodes and edges

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.
media.caption: The shortest path to the crown jewel is length 3. Break the choke point and the campaign dies.
media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.
media.title: Kill chain as a graph

media.alt: A policy engine at the center of a small graph evaluates an access request from a finance user on an untrusted laptop to an R and D code server. The request is denied because there is no prior relationship edge and the device is untrusted.
media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.
media.title: Zero Trust runs on relationships
ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.

media.title: UEBA: baseline vs deviation
media.caption: UEBA learns each user's normal hours, locations, and volumes, then scores deviations from that baseline.
media.alt: 24-hour timeline showing a shaded normal login window from 8 AM to 6 PM with normal logins inside it, and a red anomaly marker at 2:47 AM for a foreign login scoring 97 out of 100.
